This ended up being a bit harder than I expected. Im documenting why here, and then we can decide what to do. 

The generate command takes a source and a destination. When the code was originally written there was no concept of fetching a file from a remote URL. The source as is, creates a full path from your local machine to the file in the repo. 

for example,  kameronkales/desktop/counterfact/petstore.yaml

However, if you try to feed a URL into the generate command you end up with something like this 

kameronkales/desktop/counterfact/https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OAI/OpenAPI-Specification/main/examples/v3.0/petstore.yaml

Internally counterfact tries to split the full path into multiple pieces. One of which being a basePath. That works fine when the file is local, but blows up when it builds a reference like this 

kameronkales/desktop/counterfact/https://raw.githubusercontent.com/OAI/OpenAPI-Specification/main/examples/v3.0

and 

petstore.yaml

After talking with Patrick, we're going to remove basePath as it exists today and refactor to use this. 

https://swagger.io/docs/specification/using-ref/

This will let us handle remote URIs and local the same. Im going to create a separate story to rip out basePath and get working with this new URI concept, then come back to this once it works.

The default implementation could be `return response.random();`

These are equivalent (assuming 200 is a valid response code and the accepts header lists "application/json" first). 

```ts
response.random()

```

These are also equivalent:

```ts
response({message: "hello"})
response["200_OK"]({message: "hello"})

```

I can't decide if I love or hate that response is both a callable and an object. It may be better to be more explicit. 

```ts
response.create({message: "hello"})

response["200_OK"]["application/json"].create({message: "hello"})
```

Okay now that I'm looking at it I like `create()` better. A tiny bit more verbose but the cognitive load is lighter.

That chaining syntax could be enforced by the type system. If there are multiple content types, you don't get a `create()` function. You have to use `match()`. After using `match()` you continue to only get `match()` until all content types are used up. When the last type is used up you don't get another `match()` function. You're at the end and the return type is now a response object (`{ status, headers, body}`). Which means the extra `create()` at the end to make the types line up is no longer necessary.

I don't like `create()`. It feels out of place. Instead we could have `response.json(body, headers?)` aliased to `response.match('application/json', body, headers?)`. And similar for the other most comment content types: text, csv, xml, etc.

Got it mostly working working but taking a step back.

Currently the API looks like this: 

```ts
function GET({response}) {
   return response["200"]
      .json({name: "Fido"}, {  "x-some-header": "value",  "x-another-header": "value" } )
      .text("Fido", {  "x-some-header": "value",  "x-another-header": "value" } )
}

Somehow I got the idea that response headers are attached to a media type and made things unnecessarily difficult for myself. The API should look like this.

```ts
function GET({response}) {
   return response["200"]
      .header( "x-some-header", "value")
      .header( "x-another-header", "value")
      .json({name: "Fido"})
      .text("Fido")
}
``` 

I didn't fully realize it until I got this deep, but I'm trying to solve several problems at once. Some of them apply to the server running in JavaScript:

1. A fluent API for building a response that is nothing more than an alternative way to create the `{status, headers, contentType, body}` object. (#133)
2. Handle multiple response types in the same return statement (without `if (accepts(...)))). That can be accomplished by making the response look like `{status, headers, format: `{"application/json": body, "text/plain: body...} } }` instead of `{status, headers, contentType, body}`, but only when multiple media types are present. (#134)
4. Simplify the generated code (which the point above will do) 
5. Ability to have `return response[200].random()` which will also simplify the generated code. (#135)
6. Ability to add a description to the status code `response["418_I_AM_A_TEAPOT"]` instead of `response[418]`. This is mostly useful for TypeScript but it needs to start with the JS code in the server. (#133)
7. Option for the body to be lazily evaluated. It could be a function or an async function or a generator. (#137)


And some of them apply to the types system and code generator. See #136

156.body:
```ts
export { MODEL } from '../parent.js'; 
```

This might cause a slight inconsistency with hot-reloading.

1. On load `/paths/a.ts` exists.
2. Make a change to the `MODEL` in `/paths/a.ts`
3. Make a change to the OpenAPI document, generate code, and now `/paths/a/b.ts` is created with a reference to `MODEL` from `/paths/a.ts`. It will be a reference to the _new_ version of `MODEL`. 

Now that I've written that out I think this is a weird edge case and not a big deal. But we could work around it. When `b.js` is loaded, check if the exported object is the same object that was imported (but not used) from the updated `a.js`. If so, use the _original_ model from `a.js` instead of the new one.

There also may be a possibility to respond to a change in the model by adding any new properties without overwriting existing properties. 

```js
const liveModel = {...updatedModel, ...liveModel}
```

Instead of sticking the `MODEL` in a paths file, it might make more sense to have a file with a special name like `$MODEL.js` which has the model for all endpoints in that directory (and subdirectories, if they don't provide their own `$MODEL.js`). 

That means `./paths/a.js` and `./paths/b.js` would have to share the same model. That's probably okay most of the time. A couple of ways to work around that.

1. To give `b` a different model, `export const b` from `$MODEL.js`. The default export will apply to any files that don't have a corresponding variable. 
2. An optional file called `b$MODEL.js`

I think I like this better, with option 1. It also breaks a circular dependency with imports, which is nice. 

It _also_ solves the hot reload problem. `$MODEL.js` files simply won't be hot-reloaded. 

Oh, and it also solves another problem. By default `./paths/a/b/$MODEL.ts` will look like this:

```ts
export * from  '../$MODEL.js';
```

If the `b` directory is renamed, it doesn't break anything.

`ModuleLoader` will look for `$Model.js` files (on the first load) and add them to the `Registry`. `Registry` will store the models in a new `ModelFactory` object. `Registry#endpoint` will look up the matching model for a URL and pass that model to the lambda function. 

The `counterfact()` function will return the `modelFactory` so that we can manipulate data programmatically.

I've  landed on a clean model that unifies all three use cases without adding extra concepts.

At a high level:

- **source** → where the contract comes from (OpenAPI + optional overlays)  
- **prefix** → where it’s mounted at runtime (base path)  
- **group** → which implementation it shares  

This gives us a simple rule:

> Multiple contracts can map to a single implementation via `group`.

---

## How the three patterns fall out

### 1. Overlay

Extend an OpenAPI document you don't own using the spec:

https://spec.openapis.org/overlay/v1.1.0.html

---

### 2. Multiple APIs at different base paths

Different groups → different implementations.

```yaml
- source: ./billing.yaml
  prefix: /billing
  group: billing

- source: ./identity.yaml
  prefix: /identity
  group: identity
```

---

### 3. Multiple versions, one implementation

Same group → shared implementation.

```yaml
- source: ./openapi.v1.yaml
  prefix: /v1
  group: pets

- source: ./openapi.v2.yaml
  prefix: /v2
  group: pets
```

Both versions map to:

```
routes/pets/*
```

In the implementation, we will have a minVersion function for branching. 

```ts

if ($.minVersion("2.5") {
  ...
} else {
  ...
}
```

I've figured out how to build that function and narrow the type of $ inside the if / else blocks.

Currently refactoring the code and learning how to make this work. My plan now is to make each API mostly independent. The directory layout will look like this:

root

    /scenarios
  /identity
    /routes
    /types

````

## Agent Setup Requirements (Configuration & Safety)

### Environment Variables (Required)

The agent must be configured exclusively via environment variables. Counterfact must never persist credentials to disk.

```bash
COUNTERFACT_AGENT_PROVIDER=openai
COUNTERFACT_AGENT_API_KEY=...
```

#### Optional (future-ready)

```bash
COUNTERFACT_AGENT_MODEL=...
COUNTERFACT_AGENT_BASE_URL=...
```

---

### Rate Limiting & Safety Controls

Counterfact must enforce its own limits independent of the provider to ensure predictable behavior and cost control.

```bash
COUNTERFACT_AGENT_RATE_LIMIT_REQUESTS=20
COUNTERFACT_AGENT_RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_SECONDS=60
COUNTERFACT_AGENT_MAX_PROMPT_CHARS=12000
COUNTERFACT_AGENT_MAX_OPERATIONS=200
```

These limits should:
- apply per session
- fail fast with clear error messages
- never rely solely on provider-side rate limits

Example error:

```
Agent rate limit exceeded.
Allowed: 20 requests per 60 seconds.
Try again in 18 seconds.
```

---

### `.agent config` Command

`.agent config` is **read-only** and must not persist or modify configuration.

#### Responsibilities

1. Show current configuration status

```
Agent configuration

Provider: openai
API Key: ✓ set

Status: ready
```

2. Show missing configuration with guidance

```
Agent is not configured.

Set the following environment variables:

export COUNTERFACT_AGENT_PROVIDER=openai
export COUNTERFACT_AGENT_API_KEY=...
```

3. Display rate limits

```
Rate limits:
- Requests: 20 per 60 seconds
- Max prompt size: 12000 chars
- Max generated operations: 200
```

4. Optionally display current usage

```
Current usage:
- 7 of 20 requests used
- Window resets in 34 seconds
```

5. Optionally validate connection

```
Testing agent connection...

✓ Provider recognized
✓ API key present
✓ Connection successful
```

---

### Security Requirements

- No credentials written to disk
- No config files containing secrets
- Never log API keys (even partially in default mode)
- No fallback to unrelated environment variables (e.g. `OPENAI_API_KEY`)
- All agent execution must remain sandboxed (DSL + interpreter)

---

### Design Principle

> The agent is configured via environment variables only.  
> `.agent config` inspects and validates configuration but never mutates it.

This ensures:
- no leakage vectors
- predictable deployment behavior
- clear separation between configuration and execution

We could certainly make Counterfact handle this gracefully, maybe with a warning for invalid syntax, but I don't think we should allow Counterfact to accept this as a valid route. Do you have any agency in updating this spec? Maybe you can go to the maintainers of the spec and recommend they follow the correct syntax? If not that does make it challenging.
The swagger validator (https://editor.swagger.io/) doesn't fail the document, but it also doesn't show the parameter being recognized as a parameter.

@dethell
This is in fact no parameter - they just built an endpoint with URLs like this (and colons in URLs are perfectly valid).
Take following 2 endpoints as example:
```
POST /stuff/{stuffId}:duplicate
POST /stuff/{stuffId}:publish
```
Might not be perfect REST, but the API I'm working with has a lot of these cases.

Please also have a look at #1381, this fixed the problem of colons appearing in filenames (which is not allowed on Windows), but I feel this change somehow was not (successfully) applied to (at least) the import paths.

I guess you're right, the RFC for URIs does allow for the colon (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986). I learned something new today. We'll have to think on how to address this because we basically need to escape the `:` character with something allowed on the file system.

And if I see it correctly, there might be other problematic characters, e.g. it seems `*` is also allowed in URLs without percent-encoding, but forbidden in Windows filenames.

Not sure what a good solution is.
Map every problematic character to something else, like colon to ratio?
Or perhaps mask every "non-trivial" character somehow? (Well, find a nice defition of trivial... "small" set of characters we know are okay for filenames everywhere, like alphanumeric, braces, ...)
Perhaps just an encoding/masking for those characters that are known to be problematic for filesystems?

I think `<>:"\|?*` are the problematic characters for Windows, Linux/Mac don't really have problematic characters (perhaps just the null character) - and `/` is handled in a special way anyways.
Now we can discuss what is allowed in a URL and what some more or less sane developers might put in it anyways..

See here for even more interesting stuff about what might not be allowed on Windows:
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/naming-a-file#naming-conventions

Thanks for reporting this issue!

The colon in particular has come up before: https://github.com/pmcelhaney/counterfact/issues/1381

Let's start by making sure that works all the way through.
